sentences.text: Scientists estimated that this dinosaur measured 15 meters in length and weighed 5 metric tons.
It stood 4 meters tall, representing a relatively small sauropod for its geological period.
The skull features a mysterious second opening near the nose, a trait absent in Diplodocus and its close relatives.
Its tail terminated in short, flat vertebrae that created a whip-like structure.
The name Suuwassea comes from the Crow language word for the first spring thunder heard in ancestral territory.
The specific name emilieae honors the late expedition sponsor Emilie deHellebranth.
Remains were recovered during fieldwork between 1999 and 2000 and officially named by Harris and Dodson in 2004.
William Donawick, a veterinary professor at the University of Pennsylvania, spotted a bone sticking out of the earth while riding with his son-in-law.
Excavation revealed well-preserved skull bones that had been partially exposed by natural erosion.
Initial descriptions placed it in Flagellicaudata incertae sedis because it showed mixed primitive and derived traits.
Later research reclassified it as a North American dicraeosaurid, moving it from the subfamily Apatosaurinae.
It shares the second postparital foramen with Dicraeosaurus, Tornieria, and Amargasaurus, linking it closely to dicraeosaurids.
This animal lived approximately 147 million years ago during the Tithonian stage of the Upper Jurassic.
Its time range spans from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
It inhabited the Morrison Formation in southern Carbon County, Montana, USA.
Finding dicraeosaurid traits in a Laurasian diplodocoid raises questions about the origin and spread of ancestral diplodocooids.
Researchers debate whether the group Flagellicaudata originated in Laurasia or Gondwana.
It is uncertain if dicraeosaurids existed before migrating from Laurasia, given the primitive traits seen in Suuwassea.
